edits.anchor: We modelled the sleep-wake behavioral sequence
Hidden Markov model of sleep-wake dynamics

paras.text: We modelled each fly's behavioural sequence as a discrete-time hidden Markov model (HMM) on a 1-minute grid with three observable symbols: sleep (S), quiet wake (Q) and active wake (W). A binary sleep/wake observable leaves the hidden state H_{1} without an emission signature of its own: in most 4-hour windows its emission row coincided with that of H_{2} or H_{3}, and transition matrices of identical likelihood then span essentially the full range of the routing and thermodynamic quantities defined below, a known property of aggregated Markov models (Fredkin & Rice, 1986; Kienker, 1989). The quiet-wake symbol gives H_{1} a distinct emission.

Sleep was scored from the 1-s locomotor counts as inactivity lasting ≥ 5 min. A single active second was bridged (set to inactive) only when the inactive runs on both sides each lasted ≥ 5 min, measured on the unbridged trace. A minute was labelled S if at least 30 of its 60 s fell within a sleep bout. Each remaining (wake) minute was labelled Q if its fraction of active seconds was below θ r_{f}, and W otherwise. The reference r_{f} is the fly's typical wake activity: the median, over that fly's wake bouts lasting ≥ 10 min, of the fraction of active seconds (count > 0) in the bout's central 5 min. It was computed separately for the light and dark phases, a bout contributing to a phase if its waking or its sleep onset fell in that phase, and over the whole record in constant darkness; at least 3 such bouts were required, otherwise the wake minutes of that phase were treated as missing (emission likelihood 1). Scaling the threshold to each fly's own wake activity makes 'quiet' a relative state, so that differences in overall activity between flies and genotypes do not by themselves decide the Q/W split. We used θ = 0.5, a value chosen after inspection of the transition-aligned activity profiles, and report θ = 0.33 and 0.75 as sensitivity analyses; every circulation direction that was significant at θ = 0.5 had the same sign at all three values (only near-zero, non-significant blocks changed sign). Recordings were truncated to whole days.

The model has *K* hidden states, a *K* × 3 emission matrix *B* shared by all times of day, an initial distribution *π*_{0}, and phase-specific transition matrices: *P*^{L} for transitions into minutes at ZT 0–12 and *P*^{D} for transitions into minutes at ZT 12–24 (a single matrix *P* in constant darkness). Within each phase the dynamics are assumed time-homogeneous. One model was fitted per fly to its entire recording by maximum likelihood, using Baum–Welch expectation–maximization in which the expected transition counts are accumulated separately by the phase of the arrival minute and the emission counts are pooled. Each fit was started from 20 random initializations (half with diagonally dominant transition matrices) and iterated until the relative gain in log-likelihood fell below 10^{-7} for every initialization, or for at most 1000 iterations; the best final likelihood was retained.

Models with *K* = 2, 3 and 4 were fitted, and the order was selected by the Bayesian information criterion, BIC = −2*LL* + *k* ln *n*, with *k* = (*K* − 1) + *n*_{P}*K*(*K* − 1) + 2*K* free parameters (*n*_{P} = 2 phases) and *n* the number of minutes; as a sensitivity analysis *n* was replaced by the number of symbol changes. A fly was flagged, not excluded, when *K* = 2 or 4 improved BIC over *K* = 3 by more than 10. Routing and thermodynamic quantities are defined for *K* = 3. The three states were labelled by their emissions: H_{3} has the largest P(S | H), H_{2} the larger P(W | H) of the remaining two, and H_{1} is the third. H_{1} was considered unidentified in a fly if its emission row lay within total-variation distance 0.05 of the row of H_{2} or H_{3}; such flies were excluded from routing and thermodynamic summaries and counted.

Single 4-hour windows were not fitted separately, because one window does not contain enough sleep–wake transitions to resolve routing: on synthetic sequences with a distinct H_{1} and known routing, a single 240-minute window selected *K* = 3 in only 4% of cases and gave routing fractions with a standard deviation of 0.75 (Validation of the inference, below). As a secondary design with finer time resolution, CS, *per0* (LD) and *fumin* flies were also fitted with four transition matrices, one for each 6-hour block (ZT 0–6, 6–12, 12–18, 18–24), with shared emissions.
Model-free cycle current

To obtain a direction of circulation that does not depend on any HMM, each sleep onset and each waking was classified directly from the 1-s counts. For every wake bout lasting ≥ 10 min between two sleep bouts, the active fraction in seconds 61–300 after the waking (exit) and in seconds 61–300 before the next sleep onset (approach) was labelled Q if below θ r_{f} and A (active) otherwise, with r_{f} as defined above for the phase of the transition; the first minute next to each transition was excluded because it contains a movement by definition. The model-free current is *c* = P(Q | onset) − P(Q | waking), computed per fly and light phase. Positive *c* indicates the forward cycle A → Q → S → A, which corresponds to H_{2} → H_{1} → H_{3} → H_{2}, i.e. the forward direction of *J*_{cycle} defined below.
Round trips around sleep bouts

Each sleep bout was classified by its entry and exit route into one of four round-trip types: forward (quiet entry, active exit; Q → S → A), reverse (A → S → Q), direct (A → S → A) and quiet on both sides (Q → S → Q). At the level of observed behaviour, sleep bouts flanked on both sides by wake bouts lasting ≥ 10 min were used, entry and exit being classified as in the model-free cycle current, with r_{f} of the phase of the sleep onset. At the hidden level, the same four types were counted on each posterior path for visits to H_{3} lasting ≥ 5 min that were preceded and followed by ≥ 10 min without H_{3} (the definition matched to the behavioural one), with H_{1} in the role of Q and H_{2} in the role of A; fractions were computed per path and averaged over paths. A round trip was assigned to the phase of its sleep onset; flies needed at least 3 round trips in a phase. For each fly and phase we report the fraction and the rate per hour of each type, the marginal probabilities of a quiet entry and a quiet exit, and the difference between each type's fraction and the product of the marginals (a test of whether entry and exit routes are independent). Forward and reverse fractions were compared within flies by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected over genotype–phase blocks.
Dependence of routing on bout duration

To test whether the choice of route depends on the history of the bout, three relations were examined for each sleep bout: R1, whether the exit was quiet (Q, or H_{1} at the hidden level) or active (A, or H_{2}) against the duration of the sleep bout it ended; R2, whether the entry was quiet or active against the duration of the preceding wake period; and R3, the entry route against the duration of the sleep bout it began. In a Markov model the exit route from a state is independent of the time spent in it, so a dependence in R1 is a direct departure from the Markov description. At the level of observed behaviour, sleep bouts (bridged scoring) were used; an exit was classified only if the following wake bout lasted ≥ 10 min and an entry only if the preceding one did, by comparing the active fraction in seconds 61–300 after waking (before onset) with θ r_{f} as in the model-free cycle current. At the hidden level, visits to H_{3} lasting ≥ 5 min with a previous and a next visit were used on each of 200 posterior paths, an entry (exit) being classified when the gap since the previous (until the next) H_{3} visit was ≥ 10 min, the neighbouring state giving the route. A bout was assigned to the light phase of its onset.

For each fly and phase, the effect was summarised as *D* = ⟨ln *t*⟩_{quiet} − ⟨ln *t*⟩_{active}, the difference between the mean log durations of bouts with a quiet and with an active route, requiring at least two bouts of each kind; *D* < 0 means that quiet routes go with shorter bouts. At the hidden level *D* was computed on each posterior path and averaged over the paths on which it was defined (at least half). The group statistic was the mean of *D* over flies. At the observed level its null distribution was obtained by permuting the route labels among each fly's own bouts within the phase (2000 permutations), which preserves each fly's durations and route frequencies and removes only their association; because the comparison is made within flies, differences between flies cannot produce an effect. At the hidden level the null was obtained from 400 records simulated from each fly's fitted model and decoded with the same procedure, which gives the value expected from a Markov process through the full pipeline. Two-sided p-values were Holm-corrected over genotype–phase blocks, separately for each relation and level. For illustration, the probability of a quiet route was also plotted in fixed duration bins (sleep 5–10, 10–20, 20–40, 40–80, > 80 min; wake 10–20, 20–40, 40–80, 80–160, > 160 min), weighting flies equally and showing only bins to which at least 10 flies contributed; these binned curves are descriptive.

edits.anchor: We define the routing fraction as the proportion
We define the routing fraction as the proportion

paras.text: We define the routing fraction as the proportion of Sleep→Wake transitions that travel via the indirect path (H_{3} → H_{1} → H_{2}) rather than the direct path (H_{3} → H_{2}), and analogously for Wake→Sleep. Route counts were obtained from the posterior distribution of hidden paths rather than from the single most probable (Viterbi) path, because a functional of the most probable path is a biased estimator of the posterior expectation of that functional. For each fly, 200 hidden paths spanning the whole recording were drawn under the fitted model by forward filtering–backward sampling, so no window boundaries enter the counting. Each sampled path was run-length compressed, and the direct and indirect Sleep→Wake counts (*N*_{32}, *N*_{312}) and Wake→Sleep counts (*N*_{23}, *N*_{213}) were obtained by matching the corresponding two- or three-entry patterns, which requires the matched trajectory to begin and end at Sleep/Wake (or Wake/Sleep) with no other intervening state. Each route was assigned to the light phase (or 6-hour block) of the minute in which it completes. The directed single-step counts *N*_{ij} used below were taken from the same compressed paths.

Every nonlinear function of the counts (the routing fractions, Eqs. 14–15, and the entropy production, Eq. 22) was evaluated on each sampled path and then averaged over the 200 paths, respecting Jensen's inequality. On a given path a routing fraction required at least 3 routes in its denominator; a fly's value was reported if it was defined on at least half of its paths. Viterbi counts were computed for comparison only. In the S/Q/W analysis the model-predicted routing fractions (Eq. 16) were computed from the phase matrices *P*^{L} and *P*^{D} rather than per window.

paras.text: In the S/Q/W analysis, *N*_{32} and *N*_{23} were counted on each posterior path and divided by the number of recorded hours in the phase (or block), *T*_{phase}. Because *J*_{cycle} is linear in the counts, its posterior mean equals Eq. (20) evaluated on the posterior-mean counts. The model-based stationary flux of each phase matrix, *J* = π_{2}*P*(2,1) − π_{1}*P*(1,2) per step, converted to transitions per hour, agreed with the count-based value (per-fly Spearman correlation 0.93–1.00 in every genotype and phase). For a three-state chain, the sign of *J*_{cycle} equals the sign of the cycle affinity (Eq. 21) and of the routing difference (*F*_{W→S} − *F*_{S→W})/2 computed from the same matrix, so all three report the same direction of circulation. A phase in which one edge of the cycle was numerically absent (|*J*| < 10^{-12}) carries no cycle and was excluded from directional analyses.

edits.anchor: where  is the total count of  transitions

paras.text: In the S/Q/W analysis, Eq. (22) was evaluated on each posterior path, with *T*_{phase} in place of *T*_{valid}, and then averaged over paths. The observability gate was replaced by a bound. An edge pair traversed in one direction only (count *k* in one direction, 0 in the other) states that the reverse rate is below the detection limit; at 95% confidence that limit is 3 transitions over the recording (the Poisson zero-count limit, or rule of three). The edge term (*k* − *b*) ln(*k*/*b*) decreases monotonically in the unobserved count *b* and vanishes at *b* = *k*, so its minimum over the permitted range 0 ≤ *b* ≤ 3 lies at *b*^{∗} = min(3, *k*). The term therefore becomes (*k* − 3) ln(*k*/3) for *k* > 3 and 0 otherwise. Substituting *b*^{∗} in both the prefactor and the logarithm makes each such edge term a 95% lower bound given the observed forward count, and the sum non-negative by construction; it coincides with Eq. (22) whenever both directions are observed. The estimator as a whole is not a lower bound on the true rate: with finite counts the Schnakenberg sum is biased upward when the true irreversibility is small (Validation of the inference, item vii). Model-based entropy production per phase was computed from the fitted transition matrix at its stationary distribution, and was reported as infinite when a transition was present in one direction only.

edits.anchor: Onsager linear response and thermodynamic conductance

paras.text: Validation of the inference

Every inference step was tested on synthetic data before it was applied to flies, with pass criteria fixed in advance. (i) Positive control: 20 synthetic flies (4 days each) were generated from a three-state model with a distinct H_{1} emission and known phase-specific routing (light *F*_{S→W} = −0.3, *F*_{W→S} = +0.4; dark +0.2 and −0.1) and refitted. BIC selected *K* = 3 in all flies, and the routing fractions were recovered with bias ≤ 0.03 and standard deviation 0.20–0.27. (ii) Negative controls: two-state truths without H_{1}, with and without a factor-of-two drift of the exit rates across each 12-hour phase, selected *K* = 2 in all flies, so neither a missing state nor within-phase drift was mistaken for H_{1}. (iii) Reversible null: a three-state truth obeying detailed balance in both phases gave fitted cycle currents of zero within ±0.03, so the procedure does not create circulation; the fitted entropy production of such reversible flies reached 0.26–0.33 nats h^{-1} (95th percentile), which we take as the noise floor for single-fly values.

(iv) Per-fly precision: for 5 flies per genotype, 30 records simulated from each fly's fitted model were refitted (parametric bootstrap), giving the standard deviation of single-fly routing fractions. (v) Posterior-predictive checks: records simulated from each fly's fitted model were compared with the data, both for the fractions of S, Q and W minutes and the number of symbol changes in every 4-hour window, and for the observable current *c*_{obs} = P(Q | last wake minute before a sleep onset) − P(Q | first wake minute after a waking). The latter also gives the expected ratio between the hidden current and the observable current under coarse-graining. (vi) For the 6-hour design, 20 records simulated from each of 5 flies' fitted models per genotype were refitted with the 6-hour model; the design was deemed usable for a genotype if the median standard deviation of its routing fractions was below 0.3 in every block, which held for CS and *per0* (LD) but not for *fumin*. (vii) Entropy-production estimators: for every fly, 20 records simulated from its fitted model were analysed with the count-based estimators at the hidden level (posterior paths decoded with the true parameters) and at the observable level (S/Q/W symbols), and compared with the model's exact stationary entropy production. For flies whose fitted model has every transition in both directions, the hidden estimator exceeded the exact value by a roughly constant +0.01 to +0.025 nats h^{-1}, negligible where circulation is strong but comparable to the value itself where it is weak. For flies whose fitted model has a transition in one direction only (17–36% of *fumin* and *sss* flies), the exact value is infinite or very large while the count estimator remains small. Entropy production and the hidden–observable difference were therefore interpreted only in phases with substantial circulation.
Changes in the direction of circulation

For the 6-hour design, the per-fly routing difference *c*_{b} = (*F*_{W→S} − *F*_{S→W})/2 in block *b*, whose sign is the direction of *J*_{cycle}, was tested against zero in each block by a one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Holm-corrected over the four blocks). Change across the day was tested by a Friedman test over the four blocks, followed by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on within-fly differences between adjacent blocks (Holm-corrected). A change of direction was claimed only if two blocks had significant group directions of opposite sign that also differed significantly within flies. Changes across days were assessed by refitting the first and second halves of each fly's recording separately. Whether more flies changed sign than expected from estimation noise alone was tested against each fly's sign-flip probability under a no-change null: 8 records were simulated from the fly's whole-record model, split and refitted in the same way, and the observed number of flips was compared with the resulting Poisson-binomial distribution. The same no-change simulations, analysed with the within-phase Wilcoxon tests, were used to verify that the 6-hour estimator does not by itself create differences between blocks.

In the S/Q/W analysis, entropy production and cycle flux were related per fly and light phase rather than per genotype mean. Each point is one fly in one phase: *J*_{cycle} is the count-based flux (Eq. 20) averaged over the posterior paths, and EPR is the rule-of-three bound (Entropy production rate) computed on each path and averaged. Fly–phases with no cycle (|*J*| < 10^{-12}) or without a Q/W reference were excluded. For each genotype, light and dark phases pooled, two descriptions were compared by least squares with a free intercept *b*: constant cycle affinity, EPR = *b* + *a*|*J*_{cycle}|, with *a* the typical affinity in nats per cycle; and linear response, EPR = *b* + *J*_{cycle}^{2}/*L*. The free intercept absorbs the additive offset of the count estimator (≈ 0.01–0.025 nats h^{-1}, Validation item vii) and is not given a physical interpretation. Both descriptions have two parameters and were compared by their residual sums of squares. The exponent *n* of EPR ∝ |*J*_{cycle}|^{n} was estimated as the slope of ln(EPR − 0.02) on ln|*J*_{cycle}| over points with |*J*_{cycle}| ≥ 0.05 cycles h^{-1} and EPR ≥ 0.05 nats h^{-1}; *n* ≈ 1 indicates constant affinity and *n* ≈ 2 linear response.

The Onsager conductance was then estimated as in Eq. (25), by ordinary least squares of EPR on *J*_{cycle}^{2} through the origin, per genotype, both pooled over phases and per phase, with *L* = 1/slope, its standard error by error propagation and its 95% interval by inverting the interval of the slope. Because the light and dark points of a fly are not independent, intervals were also obtained by a bootstrap over flies (2000 resamples, each fly's phases kept together), and genotypes were compared with the control by the bootstrap distribution of the difference in *L*; the Wald test on the slope is reported alongside but overstates significance for this reason. Subtracting the calibrated estimator offset (0.02 nats h^{-1}) before the fit changed *L* by 1–6%, and fitting with a free intercept instead of through the origin changed the slope by 2–5% (16% in *fumin*); neither changed the ordering of genotypes. For a single edge with one-way traffic *N* (transitions h^{-1}) and net current *J*, the Schnakenberg term is *J* ln[(*N* + *J*/2)/(*N* − *J*/2)] ≈ *J*^{2}/*N* when *J* ≪ *N*; a quadratic relation between EPR and *J*_{cycle} therefore indicates net currents that are small relative to the back-and-forth traffic on each edge, even when the summed cycle affinity is of order one nat per cycle.

Specific to per-window fits at 1-s resolution. The S/Q/W analysis uses no P_min gate: zero counts get the rule-of-three bound (Entropy production rate), and a transition absent in one direction is reported as infinite / no cycle. Keep only if the per-window sections are kept.

All quantities here come from per-window binary-model matrices; state energies and barriers involving H1 are not identified in windows where H1 is degenerate. Recompute from the S/Q/W phase matrices or drop.

The boundary values (F = -1 in most fumin and sss flies) come from Viterbi counts of the binary model. In the S/Q/W model, fumin and sss routing fractions are interior (e.g. fumin light F_S->W = -0.50). Update or remove.

comments.text: In the binary model, a per0 fly's position in (F_S->W, F_W->S) is predicted by how often its degenerate H1 copied the SLEEP emission row (Spearman -0.94, 25 flies; RESULTS_LEDGER, post hoc). In the S/Q/W model per0 forms one group (85-89% of flies with forward circulation, LD and DD). Recommend removing this section and the subgroup comparisons in 'Group comparisons'.
